newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-THE NUMBERS SAY IT WILL BE TYSON OVER SELDON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-THE NUMBERS SAY IT WILL BE TYSON OVER SELDON.

text.p: Numbers don't lie, and the numbers that built this town from a desert watering hole to a mecca for gamblers say Mike Tyson can mail in his victory over Bruce Seldon on Saturday night.
The oddsmakers' numbers say Tyson is now a 23-1 favourite -- up two points in the past couple of days -- to win Seldon's World Boxing Association (WBA) title in their scheduled 12- round encounter.
It seems the corporate bookies are basing their numbers on solid logic that Seldon will become Tyson's 45th victim.

Probably the only reason the odds are not higher is the memory of 42-1 underdog James "Buster" Douglas knocking out Tyson in 1990 for his only defeat to win the undisputed heavyweight crown and the shirts off the quivering backs of bookies unlucky enough to have taken the action on Douglas.
But Seldon is no Douglas. By a lot.
Douglas had some very real boxing skills: an excellent jab that set up a solid right hand and a chin that allowed him to get up off the canvas to knock out Tyson in the 10th round.

It is true that Seldon will be Tyson's strongest test since he left prison in March 1995. But Tyson's exams, lasting 16.11 minutes against his three previous post-prison opponents, were nearly as challenging as looking up the first three letters of the alphabet with a dictionary.

The undercard at the MGM Grand include a World Boxing Councl (WBC) super welterweight title fight between champion Terry Norris and Alex Rios, and an International Boxing Federation welterweight bout between Felix Trinidad of Puerto Rico and Ray Lovato.
The affable, handsome Seldon, seems to have, despite his 6-foot-2 height (1.88 meters) on a body by Schwarzenegger, little to oppose Tyson.
Seldon, 29, has a very good jab and little else. His chin is as durable as a promoter's promise, and his right hand is as threatening as Woody Allen's.

Seldon's jab has been good enough to slice up the collection of boxing's lesser lights that mostly make up his 33-3 record, including his seventh-round stoppage of a faded Tony Tucker in April 1995, to win the vacant WBA title.
But when he has faced fighters with some light in their eyes, Seldon has had trouble with the glare.
Oliver McCall stopped Seldon in the 9th round in 1991, and Riddick Bowe knocked Seldon down three times in the first round before the referee stopped the slaughter, also in 1991.

Seldon, who spent four years in prison for armed robbery when he was a teenager, maintains times change, that he is a different, more focused fighter now. He claims to have had a bad right arm the last couple of years that prevented him from throwing a right hand with bad intentions.
"I am a champion, I have to have confidence," Seldon insists, sounding less than convinced.

Seldon also insists his jab will be impossible for Tyson to escape from Saturday night. The "Atlantic City Express" also says Tyson is vulnerable because his timing is still off after a nearly four-year layoff from the ring, and Seldon says Tyson no longer has the drive to be a champion.

Seldon also says Tyson's nearly two-inch (5 cm) disadvantage in height will hurt him. There also is Seldon's at least six-inch (15 cm) advantage in reach that his supporters' cite as a factor on their man's side.

But with little to fear from a right hand it would seem that Tyson, 30, will be able with unabashed temerity to get inside on Seldon, maybe work on the body if he wants some practice, and then land one of his patented leaping left hooks to end Seldon's night.
"A lot of fighters watch Mike's style and they just don't get it," Tyson's trainer Jay Bright said earlier this week.
"Mike is one of the most elusive fighters in history," said Bright, adding that Tyson has greatly improved his balance and ability to punch off of head movements.

Because of legal challenges from Lennox Lewis to Tyson's right to have fought Frank Bruno for the WBC title last March, Tyson's title will not be at stake on Saturday. Except, strange even in the weird world of boxing, if Tyson loses he loses the title.
But the figures that don't lie, that lit up all this neon in the desert, say that is very unlikely.
